column3: Ben stood by the river. The water was fast and brown, and the little bridge was very old. A bird called from a tall tree. Across the river, a path went up into the green hills. Ben held his bag close. His shoes were wet, but the sun was warm on his face. There was no road back.
column4: Beyond the last house, the path became narrow. Long grass brushed our legs, and flies danced above the hot stones. We could hear water somewhere below us, but the trees hid the river. Then the wind moved the branches. Through a gap, I saw a rope bridge hanging over the deep valley, as thin as a line on our map.
column5: Up ahead, the mountain split into two sharp peaks. Between them lay a narrow track, half hidden beneath loose stones. Maya tasted dust whenever she breathed. Below her, the valley was already dark, although sunlight still burned on the snow above. A stone rolled under her boot. Click, click, click. She listened until its final sound disappeared into the distance.
column6: Salt dried white on the ropes as our boat approached the island. Through the spray, I could make out a strip of beach and, beyond it, cliffs rising like broken teeth. No harbour. No welcoming light. Only a waterfall, briefly silver in the evening sun, marked an opening in the rock. Somewhere behind that curtain of water, the old map promised shelter.
column7: By noon, the gorge had narrowed to a corridor of blazing stone. Heat shimmered above the river, distorting the ledge we had been following until it seemed to buckle beneath the cliff. Far overhead, a scrap of blue sky offered a cruel impression of openness. We moved sideways, shoulders scraping rock, while the current shouldered fallen trees through the passage below.

column3: At the end of the garden stood a small blue door. It was in a tree, and a warm light shone under it. Red flowers grew by the steps. Each flower had a little face. They turned to look at Mia. Inside the tree, someone was singing. She put her hand on the door. It was warm, like bread.
column4: Every night, the lake turned gold. Small lights moved under the water, and the flowers on its banks opened their silver leaves. Tonight, a white horse stood in the middle of the lake. Its feet rested on the water as if it were glass. From the village behind me came the sound of bells, although the church had no bell tower.
column5: High in the branches, the town glowed with hundreds of tiny lamps. Wooden bridges joined the houses, and warm cooking smells drifted through the leaves. Below, clouds covered the forest floor. A girl passed carrying a basket of stars; one escaped and floated against my cheek. It felt surprisingly cold. She caught it gently and tucked it beneath a cloth.
column6: Nothing in the winter market stayed quite still. Glass birds fluttered inside their cages, embroidered rivers rippled across folded cloth, and a stallholder weighed somebody's dream on brass scales. Beneath the awnings, blue flames gave off the scent of oranges. I kept my hands in my pockets. Even the shadows here seemed eager to slip away from their owners.
column7: The palace had grown around the sleeping dragon, accommodating each slow expansion of its ribs. Staircases curved over scales the colour of tarnished copper; chandeliers trembled whenever it breathed. In the eastern gallery, servants moved barefoot across the warm mosaic floor. Nobody spoke above a murmur. After three centuries of uninterrupted sleep, the creature had begun, that morning, to dream aloud.

column3: Our new home was a small room above the moon. Through the round window, Earth looked like a blue ball. There were no trees outside and no birds in the sky. A little robot moved across the floor. Beep! Its green eyes looked up at me. The room was cold, but my bed was soft and my family was near.
column4: The train had no wheels. It floated above the street, carrying us between towers of glass. Far below, small cars moved through the rain without drivers. A screen beside my seat showed the next stop: Moon Gate. When the doors opened, cool air touched my face. Across the platform, a silver machine was making tea for a line of tired workers.
column5: Inside the greenhouse, tomato plants stretched towards an artificial sun. Their leaves smelled just like the ones in my grandfather's garden, but beyond the glass lay a plain of red dust. Two moons hung above the mountains. The air machines hummed behind me, keeping this small square of Earth alive. On the nearest leaf, a drop of water slowly formed.
column6: At first, the abandoned ship appeared perfectly ordinary. Cups stood beside dark screens, and a jacket hung over the captain's chair. Then our torchlight reached the windows. Outside, the stars were moving backwards through their familiar patterns. A low vibration passed through the floor. On every screen, the same message appeared, addressed to a crew who had not yet been born.
column7: Along the station's inner curve, an artificial dawn advanced by degrees, coaxing colour from the sleeping gardens. Beyond the transparent hull, the planet rotated beneath an atmosphere bruised with electrical storms. Residents rarely looked down. Their attention belonged to the quieter machinery overhead, where a faltering rhythm had entered the ventilation system: a hesitation so slight that conversation almost concealed it.

column3: My bedroom was dark, but the door was open. A thin line of light lay across the floor. Tap, tap. Something was at the window. I could see a hand on the glass. The fingers were long and white. My room was on the third floor. Outside, there was no tree, no wall, and no place for a person to stand.
column4: A sweet, bad smell filled the kitchen. On the table, six cups stood beside six plates, but we lived alone. My mother touched one cup and pulled her hand away. It was hot. Above us, a chair moved across the bedroom floor. Slowly. We both looked at the ceiling. My father had taken all the furniture out of that room yesterday.
column5: Something under the bed was breathing in time with me. When I held my breath, it stopped too. Moonlight lay across the floorboards, leaving the space beneath the bed completely black. There was a smell of wet earth. I drew my feet up slowly. From the darkness came a soft scratching, then the gentle sound of someone trying not to laugh.
column6: The corridor seemed longer on the return journey. Doors I had counted before were missing, their numbers faintly visible on unbroken plaster. From behind the walls came a steady chewing sound. I pressed my palm against the nearest patch of wallpaper and felt warmth, then movement. Something beneath the faded roses leaned into my touch, as though it recognised me.
column7: Every photograph in the hallway showed the same discrepancy. Behind the smiling family, barely distinguishable from the dark furniture, stood a figure whose face had been rubbed away. In the earliest pictures it occupied a distant doorway; in the latest, it rested one indistinct hand on a child's shoulder. The glass of that final frame was warm. Underneath it, something shifted.

column3: Rain ran down the windows of the big old house. Inside, the rooms were cold. A picture of a woman hung above the stairs. Her dress was black, and her face was sad. Under the picture stood a small red chair. Dust lay on every other chair in the house. This one was clean. Someone still sat here each day.
column4: The house stood behind a wall of dark trees. Rain had turned its white stone grey, and only one upstairs window showed a light. As we reached the door, the wind caught my coat like a cold hand. There were dead flowers on the steps. Above them, a stone face looked down from the wall, its mouth open in a silent cry.
column5: Once, the music room must have been beautiful. Now rain slipped through the ceiling onto a piano whose yellow keys resembled old teeth. Heavy curtains kept the afternoon outside. Above the fireplace hung a portrait of a young bride, her face almost hidden by shadow. Someone had placed fresh roses beneath it. Their sweetness made the damp air harder to breathe.
column6: A bell sounded somewhere within the ruined abbey, although its tower stood open to the sky. Eleanor paused beneath the arch. Rainwater had gathered in the hollows of the carved saints, giving their worn faces the appearance of grief. Beyond them stretched the family burial ground, its crooked stones disappearing into mist. Her own name waited on the newest monument.
column7: Beyond the drawing room's shuttered windows, the sea worried at the foundations with the persistence of an old accusation. Inside, everything suggested a departure endlessly postponed: gloves beside a sealed letter, a travelling trunk furred with dust. Above the mantelpiece, the ancestral portraits had darkened almost beyond recognition. Only their hands remained distinct, pale against the varnish, gripping books, flowers, one another.

column3: The classroom was empty. Sunlight fell on the desks, and the clock made a soft tick, tick. On our teacher's chair sat a wet blue bag. Water ran from it onto the floor. Outside, the playground was dry. There was no rain today. I looked at the open window. A small fish lay on the desk next to it.
column4: Nothing in the little shop was broken. The shelves were full, the door was locked, and yesterday's newspaper lay beside the till. Yet every clock showed a different time. Near the back wall, one clean square stood out on the dusty floor. Something heavy had stood there. A narrow line of fresh mud led from that space to the locked door.
column5: Morning light revealed three cups on the garden table. Two held cold tea; the third was empty and perfectly clean. Beneath it, the wood was dry, although last night's rain had soaked everything else. Leila crouched beside the chairs. Only two sets of footprints crossed the soft lawn, both leading towards the table. Neither set led back to the house.
column6: Dust softened every surface in the study except the upper edge of the empty picture frame. Beneath it, a pale rectangle marked the wallpaper. There was no broken glass, no overturned furniture, no obvious sign of haste. On the desk, however, the calendar lay open at tomorrow's date, with a single word pressed so deeply into the paper that the page beneath was torn.
column7: What disturbed Mara was the room's excessive order. The cushions aligned precisely, the curtains hung symmetrically, and not a single grain of ash escaped the hearth. Only the chessboard resisted this impression of careful arrangement. One black knight lay beneath the table, its polished flank marked with white paint. Overhead, a freshly painted ceiling concealed the outline of a square hatch.

column3: Blue lights moved across the shop window. The door was broken, and glass lay on the pavement like small pieces of ice. Inside, a police officer stood by an empty shelf. A red shoe lay under it. Outside the shop, a man sat on a low wall. He had one red shoe on, and his other foot was cold and wet.
column4: Police tape stretched across the narrow street. Behind it, the shop's front window was broken, but the cakes inside still stood in neat rows. A bicycle lay beside the door with its front wheel turning slowly. The morning smelled of warm bread and petrol. Near the till, a dark line of oil crossed the clean white floor and stopped at an open cupboard.
column5: By dawn, the warehouse yard was crowded with police cars. Rain clicked against the roof of the empty lorry, washing thin trails of blue powder towards the drain. Its back doors hung open. Inside, the floor bore six pale squares where boxes had recently stood. An officer photographed them while another examined the cut chain lying neatly beside the gate.
column6: Fluorescent light flattened the interview room into shades of grey. Two plastic chairs faced each other across a table scarred with initials. Beside the recorder lay the stolen watch, its delicate gold strap absurdly bright against the scratched surface. Through the narrow window in the door, the suspect watched a cleaner mop muddy footprints from the corridor, one by one.
column7: The office above the betting shop retained an air of brisk respectability. Receipts occupied labelled trays; a framed certificate hung level behind the desk. Beneath this administrative neatness lingered the acrid smell of burnt plastic. In the wastebasket, Detective Shah found a corner of a bank card curled among the ashes. The shredder beside it was immaculate, its transparent compartment conspicuously empty.

column3: The car was back. It stood across the street with its lights off. Behind the dark window, a phone shone on a man's face. I stood very still by our front door. My key was in my hand, but my fingers were cold. A door opened across the street. I heard shoes on the road. Fast shoes, coming towards me.
column4: At the far end of the station, the last train was leaving. Its lights moved away into the tunnel. I was alone on the platform, or almost alone. In the black window opposite, I could see a man behind me. He was standing close to the stairs. Every time I moved, he moved too. The station clock clicked above our heads.
column5: The lift stopped between floors. For a moment, its cheerful music continued; then that died too. In the sudden silence, I heard shoes scraping across the roof. Dust fell through the light above me. Beside the doors, the emergency button glowed red, but the speaker gave no reply. A thin metal point pushed slowly into the gap between the doors.
column6: Below the footbridge, traffic hissed through the rain. Every passing bus briefly hid the man at the opposite end, yet he was always closer when it cleared. Anna's phone showed one per cent battery. Behind her, the gate she had just crossed swung shut with a metallic snap. The man stopped walking. In the space between them, her phone began to ring.
column7: From the hotel balcony, the square appeared almost peaceful: awnings stirring, waiters rearranging chairs, a fountain scattering light. Then the same grey van completed its third circuit. Beside the entrance, two men abandoned an unfinished conversation and looked up simultaneously. Jules stepped back into the room. The telephone was already ringing, its shrill insistence suddenly louder than the traffic seven floors below.

column3: A horse pulled a cart along the muddy street. Its feet made a slow, heavy sound. Outside the baker's shop, a woman carried warm bread in a basket. Smoke rose from the small houses. I held my candle close and watched the men light the street lamps. Dark clouds crossed the sky above the town gates. Night was near.
column4: Smoke from the steam train drifted across the platform. Women in long skirts held their hats against the wind, while a boy carried newspapers between the waiting passengers. Beneath the station clock, a soldier sat on his bag. His boots were bright, but his coat was already dusty. A whistle sounded. All along the train, hands reached through open windows for one last touch.
column5: In the castle kitchen, heat pressed against my face. A boy turned the meat above the fire while two women kneaded bread at a floury table. Outside, the courtyard rang with horses' hooves. Everyone was preparing for the king's arrival. Even the cook wore a clean apron, though a streak of soot had already found its way across her cheek.
column6: At the edge of the Roman camp, water dripped from the soldiers' woollen cloaks. Beyond the ditch, the British hills dissolved into rain. Lucius crouched beside a smoky fire, turning his sandals towards its uncertain warmth. From the commander's tent came the scratch of a stylus against wax. Somewhere in the darkness, a mule complained with a voice more homesick than his own.
column7: By the time the mill whistle sounded, Manchester's morning had already acquired the colour of soot. Cotton fibres drifted through the weaving shed, settling on shoulders and eyelashes with a softness the machinery did not share. Beneath the looms' relentless clatter, children slipped between moving parts to gather scraps. At the high windows, daylight entered reluctantly, strained through panes filmed with grease.

column3: Her yellow coat was easy to see in the rain. She stood outside the little café with two cups in her hands. When she saw me, she smiled. The street was grey, and water filled my shoes, but I felt warm. On our table by the window, she had put a small white flower in an old blue cup.
column4: The garden smelled of roses after the rain. We sat on a low wall with our shoes in the wet grass. Between us lay the book he had brought for me. A little heart was drawn beside my name on the first page. Neither of us spoke. Above the trees, the clouds were opening, and the last sunlight rested on his face.
column5: Across the crowded kitchen, I could see only parts of her: a green sleeve, a laughing mouth, a hand lifting flour from the table. Music crackled from the old radio. When she turned, a white thumbprint marked her cheek. I had known this room for years, but with her standing in it, even the chipped blue tiles seemed worth looking at.
column6: We had chosen the smallest table on the terrace, though the others stood empty. Between us, a candle struggled against the evening breeze. Whenever she leaned forward to protect it, her hand came close to mine. Below, the harbour darkened from blue to ink. I remember almost nothing of the meal, only the warmth of the plate and our gradually shrinking silences.
column7: In the bookshop's narrow aisle, he moved aside to let her pass, and for a moment their familiar awkwardness returned. Rain tapped the skylight. Around them, the shelves released their dry, companionable smell of paper and dust. She noticed that he still folded his sleeves unevenly. After all these years, that small imperfection undid the careful composure with which she had arrived.
